uncited: Custom Hardware Units refer to volume rendering architectures that utilize dedicated, non-standard graphics hardware or specialized processors (ASICs, FPGAs, DSPs) rather than general-purpose CPUs or standard GPUs .
This family addresses the demand for real-time volume rendering when general-purpose hardware lacked sufficient processing power for the highly regular computations involved .

Unlike sibling methods that leverage existing graphics pipelines (such as texture slicing on GPUs) or specific software-accelerated frameworks, custom hardware relies on bespoke silicon designed specifically to offload geometry resampling, shading, and compositing .
This family shares the principle of hardware specialization to overcome the computational bottlenecks of software-based rendering.
While specific implementations vary (ASIC vs. FPGA vs. DSP), they all aim to decouple or parallelize the heavy geometric and shading loads .

**Dedicated Resampling Units:** Separate hardware blocks handle the high-speed generation of ray starting points and interpolation of volume data, often operating significantly faster than the shading units .
**Specialized Memory Architectures:** Use of on-chip buffers, FIFOs, or precalculated weight memories to manage bandwidth constraints and ensure conflict-free access to volume data .
**Fixed-Point or Low-Precision Arithmetic:** Many custom units (e.g., VIRIM, Cube) utilize 16-bit precision for density and gradient values to maximize throughput and minimize hardware complexity .
**Pipeline Parallelism:** Data flows through distinct stages (resampling $\rightarrow$ buffering $\rightarrow$ shading/compositing) often with asynchronous buffering to hide latency .

The development of custom hardware units was driven by the limitations of general-purpose CPUs and early GPUs in the 1990s and early 2000s, which could not achieve real-time frame rates for large volumetric datasets .

Key architectures include the VIRIM system (Voxel Image Rendering on Integrated Modules), which utilized ASICs for geometry and DSPs for shading , and the Cube system, which employed eight identical rendering pipelines .
The ATLANTIS architecture later explored Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) to offer reconfigurability .
These systems were primarily used in medical imaging and scientific visualization where high-fidelity, real-time interaction was critical .
